svg.title: The same metadata makes a record credible and puts people at risk
svg.desc: The blue bar at the top states the tension carried by field records: the metadata that makes a record credible as evidence is exactly the metadata that exposes people. A photograph carrying a timestamp and GPS coordinates is strong evidence that a specific violation happened at a specific time and place. The same EXIF data, on a seized device, locates you and anyone identifiable in the frame. The two columns below hold the decision, taken item by item. On the left, keep the metadata when the value of the record lies in being verifiable and nobody in the frame is harmed by it: an empty ballot box, posted results, a queue with no identifiable faces. On the right, strip or avoid the metadata when the record could identify someone who would be endangered by it: polling staff, a frightened voter, a fellow observer in a hostile environment. Keep faces out of frame while shooting, and clear EXIF before an image leaves the device. The bar at the bottom lists four field practices.
svg.text: The tension a field record carries
The metadata that makes a record credible as evidence is exactly the metadata that exposes people.
A photo with a timestamp and GPS coordinates is strong evidence that a specific violation happened at a specific time and place.
The same EXIF data, on a seized device, locates you and anyone identifiable in the frame.
There is no general right answer here, only a decision taken item by item.
Keep the metadata
Test: the record's value lies in being verifiable, and nobody in
the frame is harmed by it
WHAT THIS COVERS
An empty ballot box
Posted counting results
A queue with no identifiable faces
Officials carrying out their duties
WHY
The timestamp and coordinates let a third party verify the
record.
Strip them and the photo rests on your testimony alone.
Strip or avoid the metadata
Test: the record could identify someone who would be endangered by
it
WHAT THIS COVERS
Polling staff
A frightened voter
A fellow observer in a hostile environment
Any identifiable ordinary voter
HOW
Keep faces and identifying detail out of frame while
shooting.
Clear EXIF before an image leaves the device, and treat every
file as carrying metadata until proven otherwise.
Four field practices
Photograph documents and surroundings rather than faces, unless the face is itself the violation and the person consents or is
an official on duty. Rules on photographing voters vary widely, so check before raising a camera.
Keep an offline, verifiable backup. An encrypted local copy synced to the mission team when the network allows survives both
seizure and shutdown.
Record counts and incidents with a structured tool. A mission form or a shared encrypted document keeps the format consistent.
Keep identities out of the record. Where a name is not the point, use a role: presiding officer, observer at station 4.
The reporting channel is sensitive in itself. Who spoke to whom and when is metadata that maps the whole observation network
even when the content is encrypted.
A record that exists only in a cloud your adversary can subpoena is fragile. Offline backup and seizure response are two sides
of one decision.
